newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria says will persist in Internet smut war.
newsitem.headline: Austria says will persist in Internet smut war.

text.p: Austria's government Wednesday played down a protest by Internet access services against police attempts to clean up cyberspace, and said providers must remain liable for illegal content carried via their computers.

Almost all internet connections to and from Austria were cut off for two hours Tuesday in what providers said was an attempt to draw attention to a clumsy raid on Vienna-based VIPnet, whose computers have allegedly been used to feed child pornography into the Internet.
"This debate has been blown out of proportion and has been used by providers to push through their own interests," justice ministry spokesman Gerhard Litzka said in an interview.
"The provider wants to make life easier for himself, like every businessman, and every law makes it more difficult for him," he added. "But the world isn't that straightforward."
The raid on VIPnet followed a complaint filed in March 1996 against one of the company's subscribers, who allegedly broadcast child pornography using VIPnet.

VIPnet's entire computer network was impounded. Allegations that police simply pulled the plug on the machines without first shutting them down prompted charges of incompetence, but the ministry said its own investigation into the matter did not back up such complaints.
Litzka said there was concrete evidence that VIPnet's computers had been misused to distribute child pornography.

The Austrian police action came against a background of increasing global unease over smut and racist cyber-content. European and U.S. authorities have stepped up pressure on providers to weed out unwanted materials from the Net.
Austrian Internet providers say it is impossible to control the amount of information that enters cybersprace through their gateways and demand a clearer legal basis for their services.
But the justice ministry said the responsibility for the Internet's contents was squarely with access providers as long as they knew what went through their networks.

"The legal responsibility has to remain with the provider if he knows what's going over his net," Litzka said, adding that some Internet access companies were fully aware of what their customers broadcast into cyberspace.
But Litzka admitted authorities still had a lot to learn about the internet. "We are very interested in a dialogue with the providers," he said. "The knowledge is not really sufficient yet."
The Austrian government plans to install a central help line at the interior ministry next month where Internet users can anonymously register pages with offending or illegal contents.
